name: Storemapper
tagline: Embeddable store locator that shows shoppers where to buy a brand's products
team: Solo founder for the first years; a small remote team (five people per Built to Sell) by the 2017 sale
timeToFirstDollar: Day 1 (3 paying subscribers at $5/mo on launch day)
summary: Storemapper is a store locator widget for brands that sell through retailers. It embeds on any website or ecommerce platform, including Shopify. Tyler Tringas, a self-taught developer, built the first version on a single long flight in 2012, grew it while traveling, and sold it to SureSwift Capital in 2017. He later became known for writing about 'micro-SaaS' businesses like it.
origin: In August 2012 Tringas was freelancing for Shopify merchants, and several clients asked for a store locator. He found no good plug-and-play option, then built a stripped-down version during a roughly 36-hour trip from San Francisco to Buenos Aires via New York. He launched it when he landed, emailed his freelance clients, charged $5/mo, and had 3 paying subscribers on day one.
howItMakesMoney: Monthly subscriptions, later with tiered plans and annual billing. It started at $5/mo; once the product matured he raised the price 80% to $9/mo for new customers, and three months later to $20/mo. He also offered $99/year annual billing to existing $9/mo customers. The early low price is his own documented lesson in underpricing.
growth: Platform app stores. Listing in Shopify's app store put it in front of merchants on a fast-growing platform.
A viral footer. The 'powered by Storemapper' link on customers' locators produced thousands of click-throughs a month.
Organic search. By 2014 almost all new customers came from organic search, app stores and the 'powered by' link. He put almost no effort into paid search ads.
Repeated price increases on new customers raised ARPU without adding more customers.
moat: Embedded widgets that are annoying to replace, plus search ranking and app-store presence. The niche was too small for large companies to target.
risks: Platform dependence: Shopify can ship a native locator or change app-store rules. Competing plugins are cheap, and a low-ARPU product with churn needs constant new customers.

timeline.event: Builds the first version on a flight to Buenos Aires and has 3 paying customers on day one at $5/mo
Reaches about $2,000 MRR while capping his time at 15 hours a month
Publishes 'bootstrapped to $50,000/year in 2 years' with a live metrics dashboard
Indie Hackers interview: ~$21K/mo, driven by targeting the right niche
Meets SureSwift Capital at MicroConf in March; the sale closes about five months later

lessons: Build on top of a fast-growing platform's app store. Its growth becomes your distribution.
Ship embedded products with a 'powered by' link so every customer markets for you.
Don't anchor on your launch price. Raise it for new customers once the product works.
A narrow utility can support a traveling solo founder and still be sellable to a SaaS holding company.

rebuild.idea: A 'find our product near you' locator for craft breweries, wineries and specialty food brands that ingests messy distributor depletion reports (CSV/Excel) and keeps retailer locations up to date automatically.
rebuild.why: Generic store locators assume the brand keeps a clean store list. Beverage and food brands selling through distributors get irregular spreadsheets, so their 'where to buy' pages go stale.
mvp: Collect 5 real distributor reports from brewery owners and write a parser that normalizes and geocodes accounts
Ship an embeddable map widget with Shopify and WordPress snippets
Charge $29/mo with a monthly 'upload your report' email and auto-refresh
Sell directly to 20 local breweries via Instagram DMs and state brewers' guild forums
rebuild.fit: A data engineer who enjoys messy spreadsheet ETL and geocoding
rebuild.pricing: Monthly subscription at $29/mo for a single brand with monthly report uploads, and $79/mo for multiple distributors, automatic refresh and analytics on 'where to buy' searches.
rebuild.market: Buyers are craft breweries, wineries, distilleries and specialty food brands that sell through distributors, reached through state brewers' guilds, trade shows and direct outreach on Instagram. Competitors include Storemapper, Stockist and Destini (formerly VIP's store locator tooling) plus free Shopify locator apps.
